pos: n. (wretchedness; the weight of trouble upon a soul; Hebrew 'amal, 'oni)
etymology: Latin miseria, wretchedness, from miser, wretched. The KJV uses it for a condition Scripture never minimizes and never leaves without an answer.
biblical_def: Misery in Scripture is real, named, and never explained away. Job asks the hardest question in the canon with it: “Wherefore is light given to him that is in misery, and life unto the bitter in soul” (Job 3:20). Zophar promises its end, though he applies the promise badly: “Because thou shalt forget thy misery, and remember it as waters that pass away” (Job 11:16). Solomon prescribes strong drink for the perishing, not for kings: “Let him drink, and forget his poverty, and remember his misery no more” (Pro 31:7). The Preacher states it as a general condition: “Because to every purpose there is time and judgment, therefore the misery of man is great upon him” (Ecc 8:6). Jeremiah keeps the memory of it deliberately: “Remembering mine affliction and my misery, the wormwood and the gall” (Lam 3:19) — and it is out of that remembering, three verses later, that he says the LORD's mercies are new every morning. Most striking of all, the misery of Israel moves God Himself: “and his soul was grieved for the misery of Israel” (Jdg 10:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines misery as great unhappiness; extreme pain of body or mind; wretchedness; calamity; distress attending want.
webster_full: MISERY, n. Great unhappiness; extreme pain of body or mind.
2. Calamity; misfortune; natural evils which are the cause of misery.
3. Covetousness; sordidness; an old use of the word.
scriptures: Job 3:20
Wherefore is light given to him that is in misery, and life unto the bitter in soul;
Ecc 8:6
Because to every purpose there is time and judgment, therefore the misery of man is great upon him.
Lam 3:19
Remembering mine affliction and my misery, the wormwood and the gall.
And they put away the strange gods from among them, and served the LORD: and his soul was grieved for the misery of Israel.
corruption_summary: Suffering is renamed trauma and handled as a clinical condition, while Scripture names misery plainly and answers it with the mercies of God rather than with a technique.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic vocabulary of the present age has more words for pain than any previous generation and fewer answers to it. Where Scripture says misery, affliction, wormwood and gall, the modern register offers a diagnosis, and a diagnosis is not a hope. The difference is visible in Lamentations 3. Jeremiah does not process his misery; he remembers it, states it in the harshest terms available to him, and then says This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. The turn is not from feeling bad to feeling better. It is from himself to the character of God.

Judges 10:16 supplies what no framework of self-management can. After Israel put away the strange gods, the text says his soul was grieved for the misery of Israel. The God of Scripture is not the impassive abstraction some suppose the classical attributes require, nor the fellow-sufferer of process theology who is caught in the world's pain and cannot fix it. He is grieved for His people's misery and He is able to end it, and Judges reports both in the same chapter.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'amal (H5999), toil, trouble, misery; 'oni (H6040), affliction; ra'ah (H7451), evil or calamity — the misery of Israel that grieved the LORD.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'amal (H5999) — misery, travail; Job 3:20, Ecclesiastes 8:6.
Hebrew 'oni (H6040) — affliction; Lamentations 3:19, paired with misery.
Hebrew 'amal in Lamentations 3:19 — the wormwood and the gall alongside it.
Hebrew ra'ah (H7451) — misery, calamity; Judges 10:16.
Hebrew qatsar (H7114) — to be grieved, shortened; his soul was grieved for the misery of Israel.
usage: “Wherefore is light given to him that is in misery” — Job asks it and God does not rebuke the asking.
“Remembering mine affliction and my misery, the wormwood and the gall” — and then, hope.
“His soul was grieved for the misery of Israel” — God is not indifferent to it.

pos: n. (hazard; exposure to death; Hebrew nephesh idiom, Greek kinduneuo)
etymology: Old French jeu parti, a divided game — a contest whose outcome could fall either way. English narrowed it to peril of life, which is exactly how the KJV uses it.
biblical_def: Jeopardy in Scripture is the deliberate risking of life, and it is usually commended. Three of David's mighty men broke through the Philistine host to fetch him water from the well of Bethlehem, and he refused to drink it: “Be it far from me, O LORD, that I should do this: is not this the blood of the men that went in jeopardy of their lives? therefore he would not drink it” (2Sa 23:17). The Philistine lords use the word of their own danger in sending David away, “He will fall to his master Saul to the jeopardy of our heads” (1Ch 12:19). Luke uses it of the storm on the lake: “and there came down a storm of wind on the lake; and they were filled with water, and were in jeopardy” (Luk 8:23). And Paul makes it the ordinary condition of apostolic ministry, in an argument for the resurrection: “And why stand we in jeopardy every hour?” (1Co 15:30). His logic is exact. If the dead rise not, a life spent in daily peril for the gospel is not noble but absurd. The resurrection is what makes jeopardy rational.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines jeopardy as hazard; danger; peril; exposure to death, loss or injury.
webster_full: JEOPARDY, n. Hazard; danger; peril; exposure to death, loss or injury.
JEOPARD, v.t. To hazard; to put in danger; to expose to loss or injury.
JEOPARDOUS, a. Exposed to danger; perilous; hazardous.
scriptures: And he said, Be it far from me, O LORD, that I should do this: is not this the blood of the men that went in jeopardy of their lives? therefore he would not drink it. These things did these three mighty men.
Luk 8:23
But as they sailed he fell asleep: and there came down a storm of wind on the lake; and they were filled with water, and were in jeopardy.
And why stand we in jeopardy every hour?

And there fell some of Manasseh to David, when he came with the Philistines against Saul to battle: but they helped them not: for the lords of the Philistines upon advisement sent him away, saying, He will fall to his master Saul to the jeopardy of our heads.
corruption_summary: Risk for Christ is quietly reclassified as poor stewardship, while Paul argues that a ministry not worth dying for proves nothing about the resurrection.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Corinthians 15:30 is an argument, not an aside. Paul asks why he stands in jeopardy every hour, and the force of the question depends on there being no sane answer if the dead rise not. A Christianity organized so as to expose no one to any risk has emptied the question of its meaning. The apostles were not reckless; they were persuaded that the resurrection made a life spent in danger a good investment, and they staked the argument on it.

David's response in 2 Samuel 23 gives the other half. He would not drink what men had gone in jeopardy of their lives to bring him, and poured it out unto the LORD. The lives of his men were too costly to be spent on his thirst. Leaders who ask others to take risks and treat their sacrifices as a personal entitlement are rebuked by the pouring out of that water. Risk in the LORD's cause is honourable; risk in the leader's cause is not.
roots_summary: Greek kinduneuo (G2793), to be in danger, to run hazard; the Hebrew idiom is literally to put one's nephesh, one's life or soul, in the hand or the palm.
roots_lines: Greek kinduneuo (G2793) — to be in jeopardy; Luke 8:23, 1 Corinthians 15:30.
Hebrew nephesh (H5315) — life, soul; the thing put in jeopardy.
Hebrew rosh (H7218) — head; the jeopardy of our heads, 1 Chronicles 12:19.
Hebrew dam (H1818) — blood; David calls the water the blood of the men who fetched it.
Greek kindunos (G2794) — peril; Romans 8:35, shall peril separate us from the love of Christ.
usage: “Is not this the blood of the men that went in jeopardy of their lives?” — and he poured it out.
“They were filled with water, and were in jeopardy” — with Christ asleep in the ship.
“And why stand we in jeopardy every hour?” — an argument that needs the resurrection.

pos: n. (well-being; how a man fares; Hebrew shalom, tobah)
etymology: Middle English wel faren, to fare well. In the KJV it is almost never an institution or a policy; it is what one person asks about another.
biblical_def: In the Authorized Version welfare is a question people ask each other. Joseph, still unrecognized by his brothers, “asked them of their welfare, and said, Is your father well, the old man of whom ye spake? Is he yet alive?” (Gen 43:27). Moses and Jethro meet after long separation: “And Moses went out to meet his father in law, and did obeisance, and kissed him; and they asked each other of their welfare; and they came into the tent” (Exo 18:7). It can be the object of a mission, and of an enemy's hatred: “it grieved them exceedingly that there was come a man to seek the welfare of the children of Israel” (Neh 2:10). Job watches it go: “Terrors are turned upon me: they pursue my soul as the wind: and my welfare passeth away as a cloud” (Job 30:15). And the psalmist prays a fearful imprecation: “Let their table become a snare before them: and that which should have been for their welfare, let it become a trap” (Psa 69:22). Behind the English word stands shalom — not merely comfort but wholeness, a life rightly ordered under God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines welfare as exemption from misfortune, sickness, calamity or evil; happiness; prosperity in the largest sense.
webster_full: WELFARE, n. Exemption from misfortune, sickness, calamity or evil; the enjoyment of health and the common blessings of life; prosperity; happiness.
2. Exemption from any unusual evil or calamity; the enjoyment of peace and prosperity, or the ordinary blessings of society and civil government.
scriptures: And he asked them of their welfare, and said, Is your father well, the old man of whom ye spake? Is he yet alive?
Exo 18:7
And Moses went out to meet his father in law, and did obeisance, and kissed him; and they asked each other of their welfare; and they came into the tent.
Neh 2:10
When Sanballat the Horonite, and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, heard of it, it grieved them exceedingly that there was come a man to seek the welfare of the children of Israel.
Let their table become a snare before them: and that which should have been for their welfare, let it become a trap.
corruption_summary: Welfare has been narrowed to material provision by an institution, while Scripture makes it the whole well-being of a person, sought by another person face to face.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern ear hears welfare as a category of public spending. Scripture's word is shalom, and it is asked after by name, in person, across a tent floor. Nehemiah 2:10 is the pattern for ministry: a man came to seek the welfare of the children of Israel, and it grieved his enemies exceedingly. That is not the distribution of a benefit; it is the personal, costly pursuit of another people's wholeness by a man who left a palace to do it.

Psalm 69:22 supplies the warning that the thing meant for welfare can become a trap, and Paul applies that very verse to Israel in Romans 11. Provision without God is not neutral; a full table can harden a man. The church that supplies bread and withholds Christ has given something that Scripture is willing to call a snare. Genuine welfare, in the Bible's sense, cannot be delivered impersonally, because shalom is not a commodity.
roots_summary: Hebrew shalom (H7965), peace, wholeness, welfare — one word for all three; tobah (H2896), good; shalvah (H7962), quietness or prosperity, Job's welfare that passed as a cloud.
roots_lines: Hebrew shalom (H7965) — welfare, peace, wholeness; Genesis 43:27, Exodus 18:7.
Hebrew tobah (H2896) — good, welfare; Nehemiah 2:10.
Hebrew shalvah (H7962) — prosperity, quietness; Job 30:15.
Hebrew shalam (H7999) — to be whole, to make complete; the root of shalom.
Hebrew shulchan (H7979) — table; that which should have been for their welfare, Psalm 69:22.
usage: “They asked each other of their welfare; and they came into the tent” — asked, in person.
“There was come a man to seek the welfare of the children of Israel” — and it grieved his enemies.
“That which should have been for their welfare, let it become a trap” — provision is not always mercy.

pos: n. (descendants; those who come after; Hebrew 'acharith, she'erith)
etymology: Latin posterus, coming after. Scripture treats posterity as a covenant category — something God preserves, and something God can cut off.
biblical_def: Posterity is what remains of a man after him, and in Scripture it is God who grants or removes it. The law reckons with generations not yet born: “If any man of you or of your posterity shall be unclean by reason of a dead body, or be in a journey afar off, yet he shall keep the passover unto the LORD” (Num 9:10). Against the house of Baasha the sentence is pronounced: “Behold, I will take away the posterity of Baasha, and the posterity of his house; and will make thy house like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat” (1Ki 16:3), and Ahab hears the same: “Behold, I will bring evil upon thee, and will take away thy posterity” (1Ki 21:21). The psalmist prays it as judgment: “Let his posterity be cut off; and in the generation following let their name be blotted out” (Psa 109:13). And Psalm 49 observes the strange loyalty of children to a father's folly: “This their way is their folly: yet their posterity approve their sayings” (Psa 49:13). A man's descendants inherit more than his property. They inherit his sayings, and they tend to defend them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines posterity as descendants; children, children's children, and so on indefinitely; the race that proceeds from a progenitor.
webster_full: POSTERITY, n. Descendants; children, children's children, &c. indefinitely; the race that proceeds from a progenitor.
2. In a general sense, succeeding generations; opposed to ancestors.
scriptures: Num 9:10
Speak unto the children of Israel, saying, If any man of you or of your posterity shall be unclean by reason of a dead body, or be in a journey afar off, yet he shall keep the passover unto the LORD.
Behold, I will take away the posterity of Baasha, and the posterity of his house; and will make thy house like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat.
This their way is their folly: yet their posterity approve their sayings. Selah.
Let his posterity be cut off; and in the generation following let their name be blotted out.
corruption_summary: Faith is treated as a purely individual transaction, while Scripture keeps reckoning in households and generations without ever making grace hereditary.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 49:13 records something every pastor has watched: this their way is their folly: yet their posterity approve their sayings. Children inherit their fathers' convictions before they can weigh them, and they will usually defend a father's error longer than the father did. That is a warning to men about what they are transmitting, and it is a rebuke to the individualism that imagines a man's beliefs are his private business. They are never only his.

The judgments on Baasha and Ahab show the covenant seriousness of the category, and the danger of misreading it. Scripture nowhere teaches that a man is damned for his father's sin — Ezekiel 18 forbids that reading explicitly, the soul that sinneth, it shall die. What it teaches is that sin has generational consequence in this world, that God deals with houses as well as with individuals, and that no one inherits saving faith. The covenant line runs through households; regeneration is still personal.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'acharith (H319), latter end, posterity; she'erith (H7611), remnant, what is left; zera' (H2233), seed — the covenant word for descendants.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'acharith (H319) — posterity, latter end; Psalm 109:13, Amos 4:2.
Hebrew she'erith (H7611) — remnant, posterity; Genesis 45:7.
Hebrew zera' (H2233) — seed; the covenant term running from Genesis 3:15 forward.
Hebrew dor (H1755) — generation; in the generation following let their name be blotted out.
Hebrew bayith (H1004) — house; the unit God judges in 1 Kings 16:3.
usage: “If any man of you or of your posterity” — the law legislates for the unborn.
“I will take away the posterity of Baasha” — a house judged as a house.
“Yet their posterity approve their sayings” — error is inherited before it is examined.

etymology: Latin solus, alone. In Scripture solitariness is normally a condition to be relieved, and the relief is a family.
biblical_def: Scripture treats solitary as a hard word. Job curses the night of his conception with it: “Lo, let that night be solitary, let no joyful voice come therein” (Job 3:7), and describes the outcasts who mock him: “For want and famine they were solitary; fleeing into the wilderness in former time desolate and waste” (Job 30:3). Israel's wandering is described the same way: “They wandered in the wilderness in a solitary way; they found no city to dwell in” (Psa 107:4). Jerusalem after the fall is given the word in the opening line of Lamentations: “How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! how is she become as a widow!” (Lam 1:1). Against all of this stands one of the tenderest promises in the Psalter: “God setteth the solitary in families: he bringeth out those which are bound with chains: but the rebellious dwell in a dry land” (Psa 68:6). And Isaiah promises that the solitary place itself will be glad: “The wilderness and the solitary place shall be glad for them; and the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose” (Isa 35:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines solitary as living alone; retired; remote from society; and, of places, desolate, unfrequented, gloomy.
webster_full: SOLITARY, a. Living alone; not having company.
2. Retired; remote from society; as a solitary residence.
3. Lonely; destitute of company; as a solitary life.
4. Gloomy; dismal; as a solitary place.
scriptures: Job 3:7
Lo, let that night be solitary, let no joyful voice come therein.
Psa 68:6
God setteth the solitary in families: he bringeth out those which are bound with chains: but the rebellious dwell in a dry land.
They wandered in the wilderness in a solitary way; they found no city to dwell in.
Isa 35:1
The wilderness and the solitary place shall be glad for them; and the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose.
corruption_summary: Solitude is marketed as self-discovery, while Scripture calls the solitary state an affliction and answers it by setting people in families.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 68:6 is the divine answer to the loneliness of a fragmented age, and it is worth noticing what the answer is not. God does not set the solitary in programmes, or in networks, or in a better sense of themselves. He setteth the solitary in families. The remedy for isolation in Scripture is a household — and where the natural family has failed or never existed, the New Testament assigns the same office to the local church, which is called the household of God and which greets its members as brothers, sisters, fathers and mothers.

Two errors are cut off. The first is the modern celebration of solitude as the path to authentic selfhood; Genesis 2:18 says it is not good that the man should be alone, before the fall and with God Himself present. The second is the assumption that a solitary person has failed. Lamentations puts the word on a city God loved, and Isaiah 35 promises that the solitary place will blossom. Solitude in Scripture is a condition to be relieved, not a verdict on the one enduring it.
roots_summary: Hebrew yachid (H3173), only, solitary; badad (H910), alone, isolated; galmud (H1565), barren or desolate — the word Job uses of that night.
roots_lines: Hebrew galmud (H1565) — solitary, barren; Job 3:7.
Hebrew yachid (H3173) — solitary, only one; Psalm 68:6.
Hebrew badad (H910) — alone; Lamentations 1:1, the city sitting solitary.
Hebrew bayith (H1004) — house, family; what God sets the solitary in.
Hebrew tsiyyah (H6723) — dry land; where the rebellious dwell, Psalm 68:6.
usage: “God setteth the solitary in families” — the remedy is a household.
“They wandered in the wilderness in a solitary way” — and He led them forth by the right way.
“How doth the city sit solitary” — the first line of Lamentations.

etymology: From plenty, Old French plente, Latin plenitas, fullness. The KJV reserves it most often for two things: harvest years, and the mercy of God.
biblical_def: Plenteous describes fullness of supply, and Scripture applies it first to grain and then to grace. Joseph names the seven good years: “Let Pharaoh do this, and let him appoint officers over the land, and take up the fifth part of the land of Egypt in the seven plenteous years” (Gen 41:34), and the harvest exceeded description: “And in the seven plenteous years the earth brought forth by handfuls” (Gen 41:47). Moses promises the same abundance under covenant blessing: “And the LORD thy God will make thee plenteous in every work of thine hand, in the fruit of thy body, and in the fruit of thy cattle, and in the fruit of thy land, for good” (Deu 30:9). Solomon's Jerusalem saw it: “And the king made silver and gold at Jerusalem as plenteous as stones” (2Ch 1:15). But the use that governs the word is David's: “For thou, Lord, art good, and ready to forgive; and plenteous in mercy unto all them that call upon thee” (Psa 86:5). Egypt's plenteous years ended in famine. The mercy that is plenteous does not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines plenteous as abundant; copious; plentiful; sufficient for every purpose; and, of persons, having an abundance.
webster_full: PLENTEOUS, a. Abundant; copious; plentiful; sufficient for every purpose; as a plenteous supply of provisions.
2. Yielding abundance; as a plenteous country.
3. Having an abundance; as a man plenteous in mercy.
scriptures: Let Pharaoh do this, and let him appoint officers over the land, and take up the fifth part of the land of Egypt in the seven plenteous years.
And in the seven plenteous years the earth brought forth by handfuls.
Deu 30:9

And the LORD thy God will make thee plenteous in every work of thine hand, in the fruit of thy body, and in the fruit of thy cattle, and in the fruit of thy land, for good: for the LORD will again rejoice over thee for good, as he rejoiced over thy fathers:
Psa 86:5
For thou, Lord, art good, and ready to forgive; and plenteous in mercy unto all them that call upon thee.
corruption_summary: Abundance is measured only in goods, while the psalmist reserves the word's highest use for a mercy that does not run out.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ordering of Psalm 86:5. Scripture is entirely willing to call material abundance plenteous — Genesis and Deuteronomy do it without apology, and the LORD is named as its giver. What Scripture refuses is to let that be the primary sense. The Lord is plenteous in mercy, and every granary in the canon is emptied eventually.

Joseph's administration is instructive against both errors of the present moment. He did not despise the plenteous years as worldly, nor did he assume they would continue. He took up the fifth part, because abundance in a fallen world is a season and not a settlement. A doctrine of providence that cannot both receive plenty gratefully and prepare for its end has not read Genesis 41.
roots_summary: Hebrew rab (H7227), much, abundant — the word in plenteous in mercy; sava' (H7647), plenty, satiety; chesed (H2617), covenant mercy, the thing said to be plenteous.
roots_lines: Hebrew rab (H7227) — abundant, plenteous; Psalm 86:5, plenteous in mercy.
Hebrew chesed (H2617) — mercy, covenant lovingkindness; what is plenteous in Psalm 86:5.
Hebrew sava' (H7647) — plenty, abundance; Genesis 41:34, the plenteous years.
Hebrew yathar (H3498) — to make abundant, leave over; Deuteronomy 30:9.
Hebrew qomets (H7062) — handful; the earth brought forth by handfuls, Genesis 41:47.
usage: “The earth brought forth by handfuls” — abundance the text will not quantify.
“The LORD thy God will make thee plenteous in every work of thine hand” — covenant blessing.
“Plenteous in mercy unto all them that call upon thee” — the supply that does not fail.

pos: adj. (many in kind; of many folds or varieties; Hebrew rab, Greek polupoikilos)
etymology: Old English manigfeald, many-folded. Not merely many in number but many in kind — variety, not just quantity.
biblical_def: Manifold means many-folded — various in kind, not simply numerous. Nehemiah's great prayer uses it twice of God's mercies: “Yet thou in thy manifold mercies forsookest them not in the wilderness” (Neh 9:19), and “according to thy manifold mercies thou gavest them saviours, who saved them out of the hand of their enemies” (Neh 9:27). The psalmist applies it to creation: “O LORD, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all: the earth is full of thy riches” (Psa 104:24). Amos applies it to sin: “For I know your manifold transgressions and your mighty sins” (Amo 5:12). Christ promises it as reward: “Who shall not receive manifold more in this present time, and in the world to come life everlasting” (Luk 18:30). And Paul reaches the height of the word in Ephesians, where the Greek is polupoikilos, many-coloured: “To the intent that now unto the principalities and powers in heavenly places might be known by the church the manifold wisdom of God” (Eph 3:10). The church is the exhibition; the angels are the audience.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines manifold as of divers kinds; many in number; multiplied; complicated.
webster_full: MANIFOLD, a. Of divers kinds; many in number; numerous; multiplied.
2. Exhibited at divers times or in various ways; as the manifold wisdom of God.
MANIFOLDLY, adv. In a manifold manner.
scriptures: Neh 9:19

Yet thou in thy manifold mercies forsookest them not in the wilderness: the pillar of the cloud departed not from them by day, to lead them in the way; neither the pillar of fire by night, to shew them light, and the way wherein they should go.
O LORD, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all: the earth is full of thy riches.
Amo 5:12
For I know your manifold transgressions and your mighty sins: they afflict the just, they take a bribe, and they turn aside the poor in the gate from their right.
Eph 3:10
To the intent that now unto the principalities and powers in heavenly places might be known by the church the manifold wisdom of God,
corruption_summary: God's wisdom is reduced to a single simple principle, while Paul calls it many-coloured and makes the church its display case before the angels.
corruption_paragraphs: Ephesians 3:10 is one of the most extraordinary claims in Scripture and it is routinely read past. God's purpose is that now unto the principalities and powers in heavenly places might be known by the church the manifold wisdom of God. The Greek word means many-coloured, as of an embroidered fabric. The local congregation — ordinary, mixed, frequently disappointing — is the medium through which unfallen intelligences are being shown the variegated wisdom of God. No theology of the church as optional survives that verse.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's wisdom is not thin. Reductionism is a besetting temptation on every side: the rationalist who wants one governing principle, the pietist who wants one experience, the activist who wants one cause. Psalm 104 answers all three by looking at the world — how manifold are thy works — and Ephesians answers them by looking at the church.
roots_summary: Greek polupoikilos (G4182), much-variegated, many-coloured; pollaplasion (G4179), manifold more; Hebrew rab (H7227), many, and 'atsum (H6099), mighty, in Amos 5:12.
roots_lines: Greek polupoikilos (G4182) — manifold, many-coloured; Ephesians 3:10, used once.
Greek pollaplasion (G4179) — manifold more; Luke 18:30.
Greek poikilos (G4164) — various; 1 Peter 4:10, the manifold grace of God.
Hebrew rab (H7227) — many, manifold; Nehemiah 9:19, Psalm 104:24.
Hebrew 'atsum (H6099) — mighty; your manifold transgressions and your mighty sins.
usage: “How manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all” — variety as testimony.
“The manifold wisdom of God” — made known by the church, to principalities.
“I know your manifold transgressions” — the word cuts both ways.

pos: adj. (not to be counted; beyond numbering; Greek anarithmetos, murias)
etymology: Latin in-, not, and numerabilis, countable. Scripture uses it for the promise to Abraham, for the sea, and — once, terribly — for a man's own sins.
biblical_def: Innumerable marks what passes beyond counting. The sea is full of it: “So is this great and wide sea, wherein are things creeping innumerable, both small and great beasts” (Psa 104:25). So is Egypt's doom: “because they are more than the grasshoppers, and are innumerable” (Jer 46:23). Luke reports a crowd of that size around Christ: “when there were gathered together an innumerable multitude of people, insomuch that they trode one upon another” (Luk 12:1). Hebrews uses it for the covenant promise fulfilled through a dead man's body: “Therefore sprang there even of one, and him as good as dead, so many as the stars of the sky in multitude, and as the sand which is by the sea shore innumerable” (Heb 11:12). But David turns the word inward, and it becomes one of the most honest sentences in the Psalter: “For innumerable evils have compassed me about: mine iniquities have taken hold upon me, so that I am not able to look up; they are more than the hairs of mine head: therefore my heart faileth me” (Psa 40:12). The same word measures Abraham's seed and David's sins — and in the gospel the first is God's answer to the second.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines innumerable as not to be counted; that cannot be enumerated or numbered for multitude.
webster_full: INNUMERABLE, a. Not to be counted; that cannot be enumerated or numbered for multitude.
INNUMERABLY, adv. Without number.
NUMBER, v.t. To count; to reckon; to ascertain the units of any sum or multitude.
scriptures: For innumerable evils have compassed me about: mine iniquities have taken hold upon me, so that I am not able to look up; they are more than the hairs of mine head: therefore my heart faileth me.
So is this great and wide sea, wherein are things creeping innumerable, both small and great beasts.
Luk 12:1

In the mean time, when there were gathered together an innumerable multitude of people, insomuch that they trode one upon another, he began to say unto his disciples first of all, Beware ye of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.
Therefore sprang there even of one, and him as good as dead, so many as the stars of the sky in multitude, and as the sand which is by the sea shore innumerable.
corruption_summary: Guilt is managed by minimizing the count, while David names his iniquities innumerable and looks past them to a mercy he cannot count either.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 40:12 refuses every strategy for making sin manageable. David does not enumerate, excuse, or contextualize; he says the evils are innumerable, that they have taken hold upon him, that he cannot look up, and that his heart faileth him. The modern instinct is to shrink the number until conscience can carry it. Scripture's way is the opposite — to let the number be uncountable, and then to look for a mercy of the same order.

Hebrews 11:12 supplies it. Out of one man, and him as good as dead, came a seed as innumerable as the sand. The promise to Abraham was measured in the same currency as David's guilt, and the gospel is the exchange: sins that cannot be numbered met by a righteousness that is not the sinner's and a people that cannot be numbered. Revelation 7 ends the argument with a multitude which no man could number, standing before the throne.
roots_summary: Greek anarithmetos (G382), innumerable; murias (G3461), a myriad, ten thousand; Hebrew 'eyn mispar, without number.
roots_lines: Greek anarithmetos (G382) — innumerable; Hebrews 11:12.
Greek murias (G3461) — myriads; Luke 12:1, the innumerable multitude.
Hebrew 'eyn mispar — without number; Psalm 40:12, 104:25.
Hebrew 'awon (H5771) — iniquity; what David found innumerable in himself.
Hebrew chol (H2344) — sand; the measure of the promise to Abraham.
usage: “Innumerable evils have compassed me about” — guilt that will not be counted down.
“As the sand which is by the sea shore innumerable” — the promise in the same currency.
“Things creeping innumerable, both small and great beasts” — a sea God can count.

pos: n. (a fit occasion; a convenient season; Greek eukairia, kairos)
etymology: Latin opportunus, literally toward the harbour — the wind that carries a ship home. An opportunity is a season with a shape and an end.
biblical_def: Opportunity in the New Testament is a season that can be sought, used, or lost. Judas is its darkest example, and both Matthew and Luke use the word of him: “And from that time he sought opportunity to betray him” (Mat 26:16); “And he promised, and sought opportunity to betray him unto them in the absence of the multitude” (Luk 22:6). Paul commands its opposite use: “As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith” (Gal 6:10). He also concedes that it can simply be absent, without blame: writing to the Philippians of their renewed care for him, “wherein ye were also careful, but ye lacked opportunity” (Php 4:10). And Hebrews uses it to explain why the patriarchs did not turn back: “And truly, if they had been mindful of that country from whence they came out, they might have had opportunity to have returned” (Heb 11:15). The door home stood open the whole time. They did not take it, because they sought a better country, that is, an heavenly.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines opportunity as fit or convenient time; a time favorable for the purpose; suitable occasion.
webster_full: OPPORTUNITY, n. Fit or convenient time; a time favorable for the purpose; suitable occasion.
2. Convenience of situation; fit place.
OPPORTUNE, a. Convenient; timely; well-timed; seasonable.
scriptures: And from that time he sought opportunity to betray him.
Gal 6:10
As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith.
Php 4:10
But I rejoiced in the Lord greatly, that now at the last your care of me hath flourished again; wherein ye were also careful, but ye lacked opportunity.
And truly, if they had been mindful of that country from whence they came out, they might have had opportunity to have returned.
corruption_summary: Opportunity is treated as a private asset for advancement, while Scripture makes it a trust to be spent on others and a door that closes.
corruption_paragraphs: Galatians 6:10 gives opportunity its Christian definition: as we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men. Not as we have surplus, not as we have inclination — as we have opportunity. The occasion itself constitutes the obligation. That is the exact inverse of the contemporary usage, in which an opportunity is something a person seizes for his own advancement and is congratulated for spotting first.

Judas shows the same word running the other way, and it is worth sitting with the fact that Scripture uses one term for both. He sought opportunity to betray him. The faculty that lets a man recognize the fitting moment is morally neutral; what it serves is not. Hebrews 11:15 adds the sober note that the door back to the old country generally stays open. The patriarchs might have had opportunity to have returned. Perseverance is not the absence of an exit; it is the refusal of one.
roots_summary: Greek eukairia (G2120), a good season, opportunity; kairos (G2540), the appointed or fitting time, as distinguished from chronos, duration.
roots_lines: Greek eukairia (G2120) — opportunity, good season; Matthew 26:16, Luke 22:6.
Greek kairos (G2540) — the fitting time; Galatians 6:10, as we have opportunity.
Greek chronos (G5550) — duration, clock time; the contrast that gives kairos its force.
Greek akaireomai (G170) — to lack opportunity; Philippians 4:10.
Greek exagorazo (G1805) — to redeem the time; Ephesians 5:16, buying up the opportunity.
usage: “As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men” — the occasion is the command.
“From that time he sought opportunity to betray him” — the same faculty, the other direction.
“They might have had opportunity to have returned” — and did not.

pos: n. (obstinate refusal; hardness of will; Hebrew qeshi, pathsar)
etymology: From stubborn, Middle English stiborn, unyielding. Scripture classes it not among temperaments but among sins, and among the gravest.
biblical_def: Stubbornness appears twice in the Authorized Version and both places are weighty. Moses pleads with the LORD after the golden calf: “Remember thy servants, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; look not unto the stubbornness of this people, nor to their wickedness, nor to their sin” (Deu 9:27). Notice that stubbornness is listed alongside wickedness and sin, not as a lesser category but as one of three. Samuel gives the other, and it is the sentence that ended Saul's dynasty: “For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. Because thou hast rejected the word of the LORD, he hath also rejected thee from being king” (1Sa 15:23). Saul had not worshipped a false god. He had kept back what the LORD said to destroy, offered a religious explanation for it, and refused to yield when corrected. Samuel names that as idolatry. The stubborn man has not merely disagreed; he has set his own judgment in the place where God's word belongs, and that is what an idol is.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stubbornness as perverse and unreasonable obstinacy; inflexibility; unyielding stiffness of temper or of will.
webster_full: STUBBORNNESS, n. Perverse and unreasonable obstinacy; inflexible temper; stiffness of mind.
2. Stiffness; want of pliancy.
STUBBORN, a. Unreasonably obstinate; inflexibly fixed in opinion; not to be moved or persuaded by reasons.
scriptures: Deu 9:27
Remember thy servants, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; look not unto the stubbornness of this people, nor to their wickedness, nor to their sin:
For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. Because thou hast rejected the word of the LORD, he hath also rejected thee from being king.
And Samuel said, Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.
Deu 9:6
Understand therefore, that the LORD thy God giveth thee not this good land to possess it for thy righteousness; for thou art a stiffnecked people.
corruption_summary: Obstinacy is defended as strength of character and integrity of conviction, while Samuel classes it with idolatry and witchcraft.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Samuel 15:23 is the passage that will not let stubbornness be a personality trait. Rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. The comparison is not rhetorical excess. Witchcraft seeks power outside God's appointed means; idolatry sets something in God's place. A man who has heard the word of the LORD and will not bend has done both — he has enthroned his own judgment and is now consulting it instead of God.

Modern usage flatters the vice. Obstinacy is called conviction, being unteachable is called having a strong sense of self, and refusal to be corrected is called integrity. The test Scripture applies is simple and it is not about temperament: what happens when this man meets the plain word of God against his own position? Saul's answer was to explain, to blame the people, and to keep the best of the sheep. Samuel's reply is the standing verdict: to obey is better than sacrifice.
roots_summary: Hebrew qeshi (H7190), hardness, stubbornness; sarar (H5637), to be stubborn or rebellious; pathsar (H6484), to press or be obstinate.
roots_lines: Hebrew qeshi (H7190) — stubbornness, hardness; Deuteronomy 9:27.
Hebrew pathsar (H6484) — stubbornness, pressing on; 1 Samuel 15:23.
Hebrew sarar (H5637) — to be stubborn, rebellious; Deuteronomy 21:18.
Hebrew qesheh-'oreph — stiffnecked, hard of neck; Deuteronomy 9:6.
Hebrew teraphim (H8655) — idols; the class Samuel puts stubbornness in.
usage: “Stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry” — not a temperament but a sin.
“Look not unto the stubbornness of this people, nor to their wickedness, nor to their sin” — three names, one people.
“Because thou hast rejected the word of the LORD” — the definition, given in the same verse.
